blocks.text: We must now say what الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec is, the word by which, as we said, other Arabs have rendered the Hebrew שפן saphan. Gabriel Sionita, in his Geographia Nubiensis, Clim. 1, section 1, interprets it as a white weasel. Golius interprets it as a hay weasel, commonly called fovina (the very learned man supposed that فنك phenec alludes to foenum [hay], and that the fovina is so called from foenum, although it takes its name from the French word fagi). For Giggeius فنك phenec is a certain very useful beast, from whose skin fur garments are obtained. But it is better to hear the Arabs themselves. Abenbitar says: الفنك حر طيب الرايحة اطيب من جميع انواع الفرأء يجلب كثيرا [col. 1007] من الصقالبة ويشبه ان يكون في لحمه حلاوة وهو ابرد من السمور واحر من السنجاب واكثر الناس علي اختلاف اسنانهم يحتملون لبس الفنك [al-fanak ḥarr ṭayyib al-rāyiḥa aṭyab min jamīʿ anwāʿ al-farʾ yujlab kathīran min al-ṣaqāliba wa-yushbih an yakūn fī laḥmihi ḥalāwa wa-huwa abrad min al-samūr wa-aḥarr min al-sinjāb wa-akthar al-nās ʿalā ikhtilāf asnānihim yaḥtamilūn libs al-fanak] Phenec is an animal whose skin is warm and of good smell, the most fragrant of all kinds of fur. It is brought in great quantity from Secalia. It seems to have sweet flesh. Its skin is colder than the skin of the simor [σίμωρ], but warmer than the skin of the sungiab. It is the custom to be clothed in this skin above all as one's age declines. Razi says: الفنك والقماقم والحواصل معتدلة في الحرارة وهو مع ذلك خفيفة [al-fanak wa-l-qamāqim wa-l-ḥawāṣil muʿtadila fī l-ḥarāra wa-huwa maʿa dhālika khafīfa] The skins of alphenec, and alkamakim, and alhawasil are of temperate warmth, and moreover light. Damir says: الفنك دويبة يوخذ منها الفرو قال ابن البيطار انه اطيب من جميع الفراء يجلب كثيرا من بلاد الصقلاب [al-fanak duwayba yūkhadh minhā al-farw qāla Ibn al-Bayṭār innahu aṭyab min jamīʿ al-firāʾ yujlab kathīran min bilād al-ṣaqlāb] Alphenec is a little animal from which a fur garment is taken. Abenbitar said that it is the most fragrant of all furs, and that very much of it is brought from the region of the Sclavi. This is how it should be read, rather than صقالية [ṣaqāliya] Secalia above (the region Sclava, that is, of the Sclavi, was once in European Scythia, toward the western Ocean, according to Simocatta, book 6, chapter 2). Ibnomar Ben Abdalbar, in the book entitled غهيد [ghhyd], that is, Explanation, says: الفنك والسنجاب والسمور كل ذلك سبع كالثعلب وابن عرس [al-fanak wa-l-sinjāb wa-l-samūr kull dhālika sabaʿ ka-l-thaʿlab wa-ibn ʿirs] Phenec, and sungiab, and simur are all wild beasts like the fox and the weasel. So say these authors; from their words it would seem that these skins belong to species of marten. Yet الفنك alphenec po[?]

[II, 417] is the Pontic mouse, that is, a species of mouse or squirrel, which Hermolaus calls the Venetian and Agricola the Finnic, after the Veneti and Finni, peoples on the Vistula in Borussia [Prussia], from whom it is brought to us for use as fur. Of these peoples Ptolemy speaks thus in his description of Sarmatia: Παρὰ μὲν τὸν Οὐιστούλαν ποταμὸν ὑπὸ τοὺς Οὐενέδας Γύθωνες, εἶτα Φίννοι [Para men ton Ouistoulan potamon hypo tous Ouenedas Gythones, eita Phinnoi]: By the river Vistula, below the Veneti, are the Gythones, then the Finni. From these Finni, I say, the Finnic mouse seems to be named, and in Arabic فنك phenec; because of its size and color the French call it petigris ^{(4)}. But also سنجاب sungiab is for Golius a squirrel, an animal of ashen color, and its skin, with which garments are lined, or rather minium (he meant, I think, herminium). Damir says it is an animal of the form of a mole, larger than a mouse, living in the tops of trees, with a blue, very soft and very beautiful skin, with which the refined are clothed. It is evident that a species of squirrel is being described. There is also simur, a kind of mouse, not wholly unknown to the Greeks. Hesychius: Σίμωρ παρὰ Πάρθοις καλεῖταί τι μυὸς ἀγρίου εἶδος, οὗ ταῖς δοραῖς [col. 1008] χρῶνται πρὸς χιτῶνας [Simōr para Parthois kaleitai ti myos agriou eidos, hou tais dorais chrōntai pros chitōnas]: Simor among the Parthians is the name of a certain species of wild mouse, whose skins are used for garments. For others simur is the marten. Damir says it is an animal like a cat, or, in the opinion of some, النمس [al-nams] the ferret, whose skin is so outstanding in softness, lightness, warmth and beauty that kings and magnates clothe themselves in it. I could add much more about both skins, drawn from Arabic books; but to explain each of these more precisely is not a matter for our leisure, and it contributes little to the present question.
The Greeks are equally inconsistent in explaining the word שפן saphan.
1. Some render it λαγωούς [lagōous]; so the Vulgate translator has little hares. We have already examined this above.

2. Others have preferred the hyena; for example Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, chapter 10, where he has Moses say: Οὐκ ἔδεσαι τὸν λαγὼν, οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν [Ouk edesai ton lagōn, oude tēn hyainan], You shall not eat the hare, nor the hyena, that is הארנבת והשפן. Similar to this is what is read in the Epistle of Barnabas: Ἀλλὰ καὶ δασύποδα οὐ φάγῃ [Alla kai dasypoda ou phagē], But you shall not eat the hare either. And a little later: Ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν φάγῃ [Alla oude tēn hyainan phagē], for which the old version has, But you shall not eat the bellua. I would prefer beluum or belbum. For thus Julius Capitolinus in his Gordian the Third: Under Gordian there were at Rome 32 elephants, 10 elks, 10 tigers, 60 tame lions, 30 tame leopards [II, 418] and 10 belbi, that is, hyenas. Yet in the Glossary of Philoxenus: Ὕαινα· ζῶον [Hyaina; zōon], bellua.
